title: Towards Model as a Library: Offline, Community-Sourced AI for Low-Resource African Languages
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 29 Sep 2026]
    Title:Towards Model as a Library: Offline, Community-Sourced AI for Low-Resource African Languages
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Large language models are frequently proposed as a route to AI-powered services for African communities, but they are least reliable exactly where the need is greatest: all African languages remain low-resource by any standard measure, and models trained on scraped, standardised text systematically misrepresent the dialectal and regional variation of how people actually speak. We introduce \textbf{Model as a Library (MaaL)}, a software architecture that packages small, community-enrolled speech models as versioned on-device dependencies, enabling offline structured data collection that cannot generatively hallucinate, for populations that current language models serve worst. Rather than relying on web-scraped corpora, MaaL's vocabulary is enrolled directly from a small number of example recordings by the speakers themselves, at the point of deployment. We describe the architecture and its central mechanism - keyword spotting that turns a closed-vocabulary text form into a voice form, filled and submitted entirely on-device - and propose transpiling the closed-vocabulary elements already present in widely-deployed digital form tools into MaaL schemas, a low-friction path to voice-first, offline data collection for the low-literacy populations these tools already reach. This is a position and system-design paper: we describe the concept, the mechanism, and an analytical feasibility case, and identify what a working implementation still requires.

report.summary: A position paper proposes MaaL, an offline architecture packaging community-enrolled speech models as on-device libraries for voice-first data collection in low-resource African languages.
report.background: Large language models are often pitched as the fastest route to AI services for African communities, yet they are least reliable where need is greatest: every African language remains low-resource by standard measures. Models trained on scraped, standardised web text also flatten dialectal and regional variation, so they misrepresent how people actually speak, and generative systems can hallucinate when used for data collection. Meanwhile, offline digital form tools already reach low-literacy populations but remain text-heavy. The paper, submitted to arXiv in September 2026 by Jean Louis Kedieng Ebongue Fendji, responds with a system-design proposal rather than a trained model: make AI small, local, versioned, and community-owned. It sits within wider efforts such as Masakhane, Lanfrica, and edge speech tooling, and argues that reliable structured data collection, not fluent generation, should be the first goal for underserved languages.
key_points: MaaL packages small, community-enrolled speech models as versioned on-device dependencies. Because outputs are closed-vocabulary and rule-bound, the system cannot generatively hallucinate, making it suitable for offline structured data collection among populations current large language models serve worst.

Instead of scraping web corpora, MaaL builds its vocabulary directly from a handful of example recordings made by the speakers themselves at the point of deployment. This keeps dialect and regional variation intact and gives communities control over what the model recognises.

The core mechanism is keyword spotting: a closed-vocabulary text form is turned into a voice form that users fill and submit entirely on-device. No network connection is required, and no generated free text is produced.

The paper proposes transpiling closed-vocabulary elements already present in widely deployed digital form tools into MaaL schemas. This offers a low-friction migration path to voice-first, offline data collection for the low-literacy users those tools already reach.

It is explicitly a position and system-design paper. The authors describe the concept, mechanism, and an analytical feasibility case, and list what a working implementation still requires, so no deployed system or benchmark results are presented yet.
report.impact: For the AI industry, MaaL reframes progress away from ever-larger cloud models toward small, versioned, on-device libraries with auditable behaviour, a direction that could influence how marginalised languages are served. For developers, it suggests a practical pattern: bundle keyword-spotting speech models with form schemas, ship them offline, and let communities enrol vocabulary locally rather than depend on remote APIs. For regular users, especially low-literacy and rural speakers, the payoff is voice-first, connectivity-free tools that respect local dialects and keep data on the device. The open questions are feasibility at scale, model size and accuracy on edge hardware, and governance of community-enrolled vocabularies.
report.tools: Watch offline speech and keyword-spotting stacks such as Picovoice Porcupine, Vosk, Coqui STT, TensorFlow Lite Micro, and whisper.cpp for on-device inference. For digital forms and community data collection, ODK and KoboToolbox are the natural integration targets. For African-language data and models, follow Masakhane, Lanfrica, Mozilla Common Voice, Hugging Face datasets, and Lelapa AI's InkubaLM. These let readers prototype voice-first, offline pipelines before MaaL itself is implemented.
